hints: Focus on how ion charge changes electron number, positive means electrons lost and negative means electrons gained.
Sodium atom has atomic number 11, so losing one electron to form $\text{Na}^+$ leaves 10 electrons, and each nitrogen atom has atomic number 7.
Add up the electrons for three nitrogen atoms, then add one more for the 1- charge on $\text{N}_3^-$ to find the azide total.
walkthrough:
**Count electrons in the sodium ion**

Sodium atom has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. The ion $\text{Na}^+$ has lost 1 electron to become positive.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$11 - 1 = 10$$

**Count electrons in the azide ion**

Azide is $\text{N}_3^-$. Each nitrogen atom has atomic number 7, so three neutral N atoms have $3 \times 7 = 21$ electrons. The 1- charge means one extra electron has been gained.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$(3 \times 7) + 1 = 21 + 1 = 22$$

**Match the pair**

Sodium ion has 10 electrons and azide ion has 22 electrons. That combination is isoelectronic with neon for $\text{Na}^+$ and very stable, which fits the ionic model of $\text{NaN}_3$.

options.A: Sodium ion 10 is correct, but azide 20 is wrong. This comes from doing $21 - 1$ instead of $21 + 1$. Remember a negative ion has gained electrons, so you add for the charge, not subtract.
options.B: This is correct. $\text{Na}^+$ has $11 - 1 = 10$ electrons and $\text{N}_3^-$ has $(3 \times 7) + 1 = 22$ electrons. Positive charge means loss, negative charge means gain.
options.C: Both are wrong. 12 assumes $\text{Na}^+$ gains an electron ($11 + 1$), and 20 assumes $\text{N}_3^-$ loses an electron ($21 - 1$). The logic for charge is reversed in both cases.
options.D: Azide 22 is correct, but sodium 12 is wrong. 12 comes from adding an electron to Na instead of removing one. A positive 1+ ion must have one fewer electron than its atom, so $11 - 1 = 10$, not 12.
